overview: This 551-page file traces Japan’s political and social transformation from the final months of the Pacific War through the first year of Allied occupation. Its 169 documents combine diplomatic reporting, intelligence assessments, translated Japanese, Soviet, Chinese Communist, and European press materials, eyewitness testimony, political biographies, party reports, interviews, memoirs, and election documents. Together they document deteriorating wartime morale and living conditions, military defeat and cabinet instability, debates over the emperor and responsibility for the war, and the occupation’s efforts to democratize government, purge militarist leaders, dismantle concentrated economic power, protect civil liberties, and foster competitive politics. Particularly extensive coverage follows the emergence of the Liberal, Progressive, Socialist, and Communist parties, constitutional and economic reform debates, and preparations for Japan’s April 1946 general election.
interest: The file is especially valuable because it captures the transition from wartime collapse to occupation-era political reconstruction almost week by week. Its unusual mixture of American intelligence, Japanese testimony, Soviet commentary, Chinese Communist translations, foreign eyewitness accounts, and party literature permits historians to compare sharply competing interpretations of Japan’s defeat and democratization. Konoe’s extended account of the failed 1941 Japanese-American negotiations, detailed observations of shortages and civilian morale, and extensive reports on party formation, candidate screening, women’s suffrage, and the 1946 election make the collection useful for studying both elite policymaking and everyday political change.
